Tasmin Pepper & the inaugural W-Series

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look at the rise of women in motorsport through the eyes of rising South African superstar Tasmin Pepper

Unique Selling Point:
Formula 1 is one of the most popular motor sports in the world, attracting a global audience of 1,7 billion people. But it's a predominantly male-driven sport with only 2 women having raced competitively in the history of F1. Now the first all-women single seater championship is about to launch in an effort to address that imbalance. The inaugural W-Series is a 6-race championship that features 18 of the best female drivers from around the world, including South Africa's Tasmin Pepper.



Summary:
Motor racing will have a new series next year, an all-female driver competition designed to promote and provide a stepping stone to overcome the sport’s huge gender gap. The W Series created controversy when proposed last year but there is optimism it will prove to be successful, long-lasting and make a difference to encouraging women into Formula One.

Further information:
Motor racing will have a new series next year, an all-female driver competition designed to promote and provide a stepping stone to overcome the sport’s huge gender gap. The W Series created controversy when proposed last year but there is optimism it will prove to be successful, long-lasting and make a difference to encouraging women into Formula One.

The series will use a 2018 Tatuus Formula 3 car, with a 1.8-litre turbocharged engine, slick tyres and a halo device as used in F1.

Motor racing is one of the few sports where men and women can compete on a level playing field. F1 has always attracted the greatest attention but has far from presented a gender balance. More than 900 drivers have competed since the championship began in 1950 but only two have been women. The last official appearance was Lella Lombardi in 1976. South Africa’s Desiré Wilson raced for Tyrell in a non-championship meeting at Kyalami in 1981 and won a race in the short-lived British Aurora F1 Championship at Brands Hatch in 1980 in which F1 cars were competing, but it remains an imbalance the W Series aims to address.

There will be six races across Europe and 18 drivers, including South African Tasmon Pepper. They will not require funding but will be selected by judges, including the former driver David Coulthard, the Red Bull technical director, Adrian Newey, and Lewis Hamilton’s former sporting director at McLaren, Dave Ryan. There will be a prize fund of £1.15m.

In this insert, we will spotlight South Africa's entrant Tasmin Pepper. Within her small frame beats the heart of a true race-car driver. Both her father and brother are also motor racers, so racing runs through the family's blood. We will interview both Tasmin and her father Barry.

Tasmin follows in the footsteps of the last woman to race in F1. She too is South African and her name is Desire Wilson. Based in the US these days, Desire has agreed to a Skype Interview.

We will also interview Tasmin's South African compatriot Ivana Cetinich, speak to W-Series CEO Catherine Bond-Moore and Race Director Dave Ryan.

We also hope to get the thoughts of F1 legend and W-Series Brand Ambassador David Coulthard, as well as the opinion of local journalist Adrian De Kock

Press Release:


Tasmin Pepper and the First All-Woman Racing Series
With a global audience of 1,7 billion people, Formula 1 is one of the most popular motor sports in the world – and yet of the more than 900 drivers who have competed since the championship began in 1950 only two have been women. The creation of an all-female motor racing series created controversy when it was proposed last year, but the inaugural W Series set to begin this weekend will see 18 of the best female drivers from around the world compete, including South Africa's Tasmin Pepper. What are her chances to top the podium and will the W Series be the answer to getting women into the sport?

Script:


INTRO VOICE OVER:

A successful racing driver need to highly skilled

Sound byte

Determined

Sound byte

& Brave

Sound byte

You also don’t have to be a man

V/O: Motor Racing is one of the few sports in the world where men and women compete against one another on a level playing field. Yet it’s been over 40 years since there was a woman in formula 1.

LINK: Now a brand new all-women competition called the W-Series is looking to showcase the talents of women drivers all over the world and provide a springboard to racing glory


V/O: And South Africa’s own Tasmin Pepper will take her place as one of the 18 drivers in this inaugural season.

V/O: W-Series is a ground-breaking competition that will see the best female drivers from around the world in a 6-race season for a top prize of $500 000.

They’ll be driving identical Formula 3 cars powered by turbo-charged engines that can reach over 240Kp/h

It’s the brainchild of W-Series CEO Catherine Bond Muir who conceptualised it as a way to overcome the sport’s huge gender gap

Comments from Catherine Bond Moore

V/O: Formula 1 is the pinnacle of motor sport but it is clearly a man’s world. More than 900 drivers have competed since 1950 but only 2 have been women.

One of those is South Africa’s Desire Wilson who in 1980 became the first (and still the only) woman ever to win a Formula 1 Race, yet still struggled to gain the respect of her male counterparts

Comment from Des Wilson
V/O: Desire is considered by many to be the best woman driver of the 20th century. Now a generation later, Tasmin Pepper hopes to follow in her illustrious footsteps.

28-year old Tasmin inherited her passion for motor racing from her father Iain, a successful racer himself.

Comment from Tasmin about being on race track since she was 2-weeks old

Intercut with Iain’s recollections

V/O: Tasmin has spent her entire career racing against men but like Desire, she too has had to deal with chauvinism and prejudice

Comments about racing against guys and being run off the track

V/O: Someone who’s followed her career very closely is respected journalist Andre De Kock

Andre on Tasmin wanting equal treatment vs guys
V/O: Tasmin raced overseas earlier in her career, but has since found opportunities harder to come by



That’s why when W-Series was launched last year, she jumped at the opportunity to enter.

Tasmin on entering W-Series

V/O: Her application was successful and she was invited to Austria for the first round of try-outs.

Tasmin on first tryouts

V/O: Tasmin wasn’t the only South African in Austria. Up and coming Ivana Cetinich was also there.


V/O: Having made it through the first round, Tasmin’s greatest challenge came in Barcelona, the venue for final selection.

Tasmin on making the final qualifying

V/O: At the end of 4 gruelling days, the final 18 was announced by F1 legend and W-Series Advisor David Coulthard

David Coulthard comment

TEASER:

DEREK: been over 40 years since there was a woman in Formula 1. Now the brand new all-women W-series is looking to change that giving hope to talents like South Africa’s Tasmin Pepper.

PROMO 1: With a global audience of 1,7 billion, Formula 1 has only seen two women race competitively in the sport’s history. Can W Series turn the male dominated sport on its head? 


PROMO 2: The inaugural all-women W-series launches this weekend. Does South Africa’s Tasmin Pepper have to the right stuff for glory?
